summary:
Fire is one of the most dangerous hazards faced by spacecraft, and fire behaves differently in microgravity. Project Phenox predicts for designers whether a material will burn in the atmosphere of a given cabin, such as the ISS, lunar base, Mars habitat, or spacesuit. We ingested NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics combustion data- 2,954 tests from 26 investigations- into Tiger Data. The predictive model selects tests closest to your chosen oxygen and pressure levels, calculates their outcomes, and provides a 95% confidence interval. It presents its reasoning (investigation, DOI, and how close the nearest test was) and returns "no data" rather than guessing.

A data visualization page creates a 3D model and interactive graphs out of the tests. It demonstrates that 95% of the flames extinguished below 17% oxygen, but there is no test close to the Mars or spacesuit atmospheres. A Mission environment page shows where each atmosphere is intended to be used, using NASA’s Eyes on the Solar System and optionally OpenSpace. The website is hosted on Cloudflare Workers. Mission Control, based on Gemini and Cloudflare AI Gateway, answers chats and phone calls using Twilio. Researchers can upload data, marked as unverified.
details:
Github: https://github.com/Nysa-Patel/flame-firewall-nasa-space-apps

Project Phenox can be helpful for the space engineers to find out whether some material catches fire or not for certain cabin condition based on NASA's real data and not on their assumptions. It is done by a Python script that gets NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics combustion data (2,954 experiments in 26 experiments) and moves them to Tiger Data. When the ISS, the lunar base, the Mars station, or the space suit is selected, the Cloudflare worker will find out which experiments are similar to that atmosphere and will count the total of these fires on the web page. It will show one of the following results – Goes out, Mixed, Continues to burn, or No data, and the confidence interval for each one is 95%. The latter is decreased if the situation falls outside of the range of the testing and the result is No data instead of an assumption across a wide range of values.

This is possible due to the use of Gemini via Cloudflare AI Gateway for reading a plain English question, querying the database, and answering only based on the evidence, and the same agent answering phone calls via Twilio. The data visualization page generates a 3D model and interactive graphs based on the test, while the Mission environment panel gives the location of each atmosphere in use through NASA’s Eyes on the Solar System and the optional OpenSpace application. Users can upload their own CSVs, which are range-checked and flagged as unverified. This was done using Tiger Data, Python, TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML and CSS, Cloudflare Workers, Gemini, Twilio via Render, three.js, and GitHub, without any special hardware needed.

This helps to make it easier for teams to acquire safe material and find out areas where microgravity fire tests have not been conducted, such as for Mars and space suits. What makes this prototype stand out is its user experience, in which one can reach Mission Control by phone number, click on the hero chamber, which redirects you to a random NASA test, and click on the bar on the chart to view specific tests in 3D. The reason we chose to use Integrity was that it uses data from previous tests and not NASA-certified ones, and because of data accuracy, as only 361 tests contain pressure data. We used verdicts with words and icons and made the site mobile and keyboard accessible.
dataRefs: NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI): microgravity combustion experiment data
PSI-69: Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX), the main source for the 3D model
PSI-159: Cool Flames Investigation with Gases
